bio.en: Kim Scott is the author of Radical Candor, the most-referenced management book on Lenny's podcast, and has coached leaders at Apple, Google, Twitter, and Dropbox.
bio.zh: 金·斯科特（Kim Scott）是《彻底坦率》（Radical Candor）一书的作者，该书是 Lenny 播客中被引用最多的管理类著作，她曾为 Apple、Google、Twitter 和 Dropbox 的领导者担任教练。

summary.en: Kim teaches that the best way to get feedback is to ask "What could I do or stop doing to make it easier to work with me?" rather than a generic request. She explains the two dimensions of Radical Candor - care personally and challenge directly. The episode is a practical guide to building a culture of honest, kind, and effective feedback.
summary.zh: 金指出，获取反馈最好的方式是问"我可以做些什么、或停止做什么，能让我们合作更顺畅？"，而不是泛泛地请求反馈。她阐释了《彻底坦率》的两个维度——真诚关怀与直接挑战。本期是一份关于建立诚实、善意且高效反馈文化的实用指南。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: If you say, "Do you have any feedback for me?" You're wasting your breath. The other person's going to say, "Oh no, everything's fine." The question that I like to ask is, "What could I do or stop doing that would make it easier to work with me?" Do not write down my question because if you sound like Kim Scott and not like yourself, then other people are not going to believe you want the answer. It needs to sound authentic to you, and if everybody can write down their question, who they're going to ask it of and then pop it into their calendar right now, this will be one of the most productive podcasts in all of podcast land.
turns.zh: 如果你问：“你对我有什么反馈吗？”那你真是白费口舌了。对方会说：“哦，不，一切都好。”我更喜欢问这样的问题：“我能做些什么，或者停止做些什么，能让大家更容易与我合作？”别把我的问题写下来，因为如果你听起来像金·斯科特而不是你自己，别人就不会相信你真心想得到答案。这句话对你来说必须真实自然。如果每个人都能把自己的问题写下来，记下要问的人，然后立刻把它添加到日历里，这将是播客界最高效的一期节目。

turns.zh: 太棒了。嗯，请转告听众，我爱他们，也很感激他们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, they'll hear this. So I'm really excited to have you on chat about all the things that you teach and your book. For people that have heard the term Radical Candor, have maybe skimmed the book, maybe even read the book a while ago, but don't truly remember or understand the concept. Could you just spend just a few minutes giving a high level overview of the concept of Radical Candor?
turns.zh: 好的，他们会听到的。所以我很兴奋能与您聊聊您所传授的理念以及您的书。对于那些听过“激进坦诚”这个术语、可能浏览过这本书，甚至在很久以前读过这本书，但不记得或不理解其概念的人来说，您能否用几分钟时间为我们概括一下“激进坦诚”的核心理念？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Absolutely. Radical Candor is just what happens when you care personally and challenge directly at the same time. And I think it's probably best understood by what it's not because we all fail on one of those two dimensions or both of them multiple times a day. So you can think about it as a two by two framework. On the vertical axis is care personally, the horizontal axis is challenge directly. What happens when we remember to challenge directly, but we forget to show that we care personally. That is what I call obnoxious aggression, and it's really important to distinguish between radical candor and obnoxious aggression. I think one of the mistakes that people often make about, and I've gotten a lot, you write a book about feedback, you're going to get a lot of it, and I've heard a lot of feedback that sometimes teams will be rolling out the idea of Radical Candor and someone will charge into the room and say, "In the spirit of Radical Candor," and then they act like a garden variety jerk. (00:05:00): And that is not the spirit of Radical Candor. That's the spirit of obnoxious aggression. And obnoxious aggression is a big problem. It's a problem because it hurts other people. It's also a problem because it's inefficient. If I'm a jerk to you Lenny, then I'm going to send you into fight or flight mode and then you literally cannot hear what I'm saying, so I'm wasting my breath. But I don't know if this is true for you, but for me, there's a third problem. And the third problem is that when I realize I've acted like a jerk, when I realize I've landed in obnoxious aggression, it's not actually my instinct to go the right way on care personally. Instead, it's my instinct to go the wrong way on challenge directly and to pretend that I agree when I disagree, and then I wind up in the worst place of all, manipulative insincerity. (00:05:48): And it's kind of fun to tell stories about obnoxious aggression and manipulative insincerity. If you watch The Office or any show about problems at work or problems in any kind of relationship really, you're going to see a lot of episodes about obnoxious aggression and manipulative insincerity. But I think the real rub comes and the fact that these, even though this is what we like to talk about, these two problems are what we like to talk about, these are not the most common problem. By far and away the most common problem occurs when we do remember to show that we care personally because you know what? Most people try to be nice people. So we do remember to show that we care personally, but we're so worried about not hurting someone's feelings or not offending them, that we fail to tell them something they'd be better off knowing in the long run. And that is what I call ruinous empathy. So that is Radical Candor in a nutshell. That's the TLDR. But please do read.
turns.zh: 完全正确。激进坦诚（Radical Candor）就是在乎对方，同时直接提出挑战时产生的结果。我认为，要理解它，最好先了解它不是什么。毕竟，我们每天都会在上述两个维度中至少犯一个错误。所以你可以把它看作一个二维框架。纵轴是真心关怀，横轴是直接挑战。当我们记得要直接挑战，却忘了表达真心关怀时，就会出现我所说的"令人不快的攻击性"。这很重要，要区分激进坦诚和令人不快的攻击性。人们常误解的地方在于——我写了一本关于反馈的书，难免会收到各种反馈——有团队推行激进坦诚理念时，总有人冲进房间大喊"本着激进坦诚的精神"，然后表现得像个十足的混蛋。这根本不是激进坦诚的精神，而是令人不快的攻击性。令人不快的攻击性是个大问题。它不仅伤害他人，也效率低下。如果我对你，莱尼，态度恶劣，你会陷入战斗或逃跑模式，根本听不进我说什么，等于白费口舌。但我不知道你是否有同感，但对我来说，还有第三个问题。当我意识到自己行为恶劣，陷入令人不快的攻击性时，本能反应不是真心关怀，反而会错误地增加直接挑战的力度，假装同意对方意见，最终陷入最糟糕的境地——操纵性的虚伪。（00:05:00）讲令人不快的攻击性和操纵性的虚伪故事挺有趣的。无论是看《办公室》还是其他职场或人际关系问题的剧集，你总会看到大量这类情节。但关键在于，尽管我们常谈论这些问题，但它们并非最常见的困境。最常见的困境是，我们确实记得要表达真心关怀，但又过分在意不伤害他人感情或避免冒犯，结果导致无法传达对方长远来看更需要了解的信息。这就是我说的"毁灭性的同理心"。这就是激进坦诚的核心要义。简而言之，就是TLDR（太长不看版）。但请务必仔细阅读。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing and we'll link to a diagram of this two by two for people that aren't visual thinkers and want to actually see it. So just to make it super clear, if you're challenging directly, basically being very candid with feedback, but it's not clear you care deeply about the person, you call that obnoxious aggression.
turns.zh: 太棒了，我们会附上二维框图供视觉型思考者参考。简而言之，如果你直接提出挑战，基本就是坦诚反馈，但不明显表现出真心关怀，这叫令人不快的攻击性。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And if you make it clear, you care a lot about the person but aren't actually giving them direct candid feedback, you call that ruinous empathy.
turns.zh: 而如果你明确表达出真心关怀，却没有给予直接坦诚的反馈，这叫毁灭性的同理心。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yes, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which of these buckets do you find most people fall into? Is there a percentage of people or companies?
turns.zh: 你们觉得大多数人会落入哪种思维陷阱？这类情况在人群或公司中所占比例是多少？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I would say 90% of us make 90% of our mistakes in that ruinous empathy bucket. It's by far and away the most common problem. But I think all of us make mistakes in the other quadrants as well. And very often we kind of, I think one of, if I'm going to offer some self-criticism of this framework, it's much easier to notice when one has been ruinously empathetic. It's almost like, give yourself some critical feedback. "I work too hard." But it's much harder to notice when we've been manipulatively insincere and obnoxiously aggressive. And maybe I could have named those things because very often manipulative insincerity is sort of self-protective insincerity. Very often obnoxious aggression is just extreme frustration. So I want people to use this framework not to judge themselves or other people harshly, but like a compass to guide specific conversations with specific people to a better place and to help us understand when we're going in the wrong direction, which we are all bound to do on a daily basis.
turns.zh: 是啊，我想说我们90%的人都会在毁灭性的共情陷阱中犯下90%的错误。这是目前最常见的问题。但我认为我们其他人也会在其他象限犯错。很多时候，我们会发现自己很难意识到自己何时陷入了操纵性的虚伪或令人不快的攻击性行为。或许我本该把这些行为明确列出来的，因为操纵性的虚伪往往是自我保护的虚伪，令人不快的攻击性往往只是极度沮丧的表现。所以我希望人们使用这个框架，不是为了严厉评判自己或他人，而是把它当作指南针，引导与特定人群的对话走向更好的方向，帮助我们认识到何时走入了歧途——毕竟我们每天都会不可避免地犯错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to talk about all those things and also how to get better at these things. But before we do that, it's very hard to change. And it's also hard just to challenge directly innately, it's hard for people to be candid, just to give people a little motivation to invest in this skill. What sort of impact do you see when people develop the skill of being better at radical candor?
turns.zh: 我还想谈谈所有这些问题，以及如何在这方面有所提升。但在我们深入探讨之前，改变现状绝非易事。直接挑战人们的固有观念也困难重重，人们往往难以坦诚相待，因此我需要给人们一些动力，让他们愿意投入精力提升这项技能。当人们掌握了更高明的坦诚技巧后，会产生怎样的影响？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: When we get better at radical candor? I mean, I'll tell you a story in fact about the impact it had on my life, some radical candor, but the sort of abstract answer to your question is we build better relationships and we do better work and we're more successful and we're happier. You ready for a story? Let's do it. Love stories. Okay. So shortly after I joined Google, this was now a very long time ago, 2004, I had to give a presentation to the founders and the CEO about how the AdSense business was doing. And I walked into the room and there in one corner of the room was one of the founders on an elliptical trainer wearing toe shoes and a bright blue spandex unitard, super tight, not what I was expecting or frankly wanting to see in the room. And there in the other corner of the room was the CEO doing his emails like his brain had been plugged into the machine. (00:09:49): So probably like you in such a situation, I felt a little bit nervous. How was I supposed to get these people's attention? Luckily for me, the AdSense business was on fire. And when I said how many new customers we had added, the CEO almost fell off his chair. "What did you say? This is incredible. Do you need more engineers? Do you need more marketing dollars?" So I'm thinking the meeting's going all right. In fact, I now believe that I am a genius. And I walked out of the room, I walked past my boss and I was expecting a high five a pat on the back. And instead she said to me, "Why don't you walk back to my office with me?" And I thought, Oh gosh, I screwed something up in there and I'm sure I'm about to hear about it. And she began not by telling me what I had done wrong, but what had gone well in the meeting, not in the feedback sandwich. (00:10:37): I think there's a less polite term for that. I'm not sure how you feel about cussing on your podcast.
turns.zh: 当我们在激进坦诚方面有所进步时会怎样？说实话，我要给你们讲个故事，讲讲它对我的生活产生的影响。先说抽象的回答吧——我们能建立更好的关系，完成更出色的工作，取得更大的成功，也收获更大的快乐。你们想听故事吗？开始吧。爱情故事。好的。2004年，我加入谷歌不久后，在一次会议上向创始人和CEO汇报AdSense业务进展。走进会议室时，我看到其中一位创始人正穿着连体裤，踩着椭圆机训练器，穿着拖鞋，身着亮蓝色紧身衣。这完全出乎我的意料，坦白说，我也不想在会议室看到这样的场景。而在会议室的另一角，CEO正全神贯注地处理邮件，仿佛大脑被接入了机器。（00:09:49）：可能和你们在类似情况下一样，我当时感到有些紧张。如何吸引这些人的注意力？幸运的是，AdSense业务进展顺利。当我提到新增客户数量时，CEO几乎跳了起来：“什么？太不可思议了。需要更多工程师吗？需要更多营销资金吗？” 我以为会议进展顺利，甚至觉得自己是个天才。走出会议室时，我以为老板会给我击掌庆祝。但她却说：“跟我回办公室一趟吧。” 我心想，天哪，我肯定要被批评了。但她开口说的不是我的错误，而是会议中做得好的地方——这可不是反馈三明治的套路（00:10:37）。我觉得对此有更不礼貌的形容词。不过不知道你们对在播客中说脏话有何看法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's acceptable, fully acceptable.
turns.zh: 可以的，完全没问题。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Not in the shit sandwich since the word, but really seeming to mean what she said. But of course, all I wanted to do was hear about what I had done wrong. And eventually she said to me, "You said um a lot in there, were you aware of it?" And with this, I braved a huge sigh of relief if that was all I had done wrong who really cared. And I kind of made this brush off gesture with my hand. I said, "Yeah, I know, it's a verbal tech. It's no big deal, really." And then she said to me, "I know this great speech coach. I bet Google would pay for it. Would you like an introduction?" And once again, I made this brush off gesture with my hand. (00:11:14): I said, "Oh, I'm busy. I don't have time for a speech coach. Didn't you hear about all these new customers?" And then she said to me, "I can tell when you do that thing with your hand, then I'm going to have to be a lot more direct with you. When you say um every third word, it makes you sound stupid." Now she's got my full attention. And some people might say it was mean of her to say I sounded stupid, but in fact, it was the kindest thing that she could have done for me at that moment in my career because she knew me well enough to know that if she didn't use just those words with me, and by the way, this is a really important point, she never would've used those words with other people on her team who were perhaps a better listener than I was. (00:11:56): But she knew me well enough. She cared personally enough to know that if she didn't use those words with me, I never would've gone to visit the speech coach and I wouldn't have learned that she was not exaggerating. And this was news to me because I had raised millions of dollars for two different startups giving presentations. I thought I was pretty good at it. And it really got me to thinking sort of why had no one told me. It was almost like I suddenly realized I'd been marching through my whole career with a giant hunk of spinach in between my teeth and nobody had had the common courtesy to tell me it was there. So why had no one else told me. But what was it about her leadership style that made it so seemingly easy for her to tell me? And as I thought about that, I realized it really came down to those two things. (00:12:41): She cared personally and she challenged directly. She cared about me not just as an employee but as a human being. For example, when my father was diagnosed with late stage cancer, I was devastated and she could tell that I was devastated. And she said, "Kim, look, you go to the airport, fly home to Memphis, you need to be with your family. Your team and I will sit down and write your coverage plan." That's what great teams do for one another. And those were the kinds of things, that was the kind of thing that she did. She couldn't do, of course, for all 5,000 people in her organization, no matter how talented you are, relationships don't scale. But she did do those things for her direct reports and the people who she worked most closely with, all of us. (00:13:27): And when a leader treats their team, the people who they interact with on a day-to-day basis with that kind of real care, then it's much more likely that their direct reports in turn are going to treat their teams with real care. Radical candor is not all about the boss giving the employee criticism. (00:15:31): So anyway, I think that the important thing for these conversations, these sort of two-minute impromptu moments of management, is to go into the conversation being humble. To me, I call it candor and not truth because if I march into a room and I say, "Lenny, I'm going to tell you the truth." I'm kind of implying I've got a pipeline to God and you don't know anything. And that's not what this is all about. This is a dialogue, not a monologue. So to me, candor implies here's how I understand the situation. I'm also curious to know how you understand the conversation. So you want to go in being humble, you might be wrong, and that's totally fine. Omniscience is not a requirement for radical candor, thank heavens. So you want to be humble. You want to state your intention to be helpful. You want to remember in your own head and you want to make it explicit to the other person that you're telling them this to help them. (00:16:25): You're not trying to be dominant or kick them in the shins or anything like that. You're telling them this because you care about them. So you want to state your intention to be helpful. You want to have these conversations right away, almost immediately. I mean, there's exceptions to everything I'm saying. None of this is absolute. But usually if I'm telling myself and Lenny, you can tell me if you have the same problem, but if I tell myself, Oh, I'm going to wait for a better moment to tell this person this thing, what I'm really saying is I'm never going to say. So if the purpose of praise is to tell people what to do more of, and the purpose of criticism is to tell them what to do less of, why wait. So you want to do it immediately unless you are so upset that you're going to say it in a terrible way or the other person is so upset that they can't hear you. But usually that's not the case. (00:17:16): You also want, and in the before times I used to say have these conversations in person. Now I say have these conversations synchronously and I'm going to recommend phone over video. 人们总是希望我给他们一份谈话指南。但问题是，如果我来写脚本，你听起来就会像金·斯科特（Kim Scott）而不是你自己，这样别人就不会真正相信你说的是真心话。不过，我认为在这种对话中，有几个关键点需要注意。首先，你需要带着谦逊的心态参与对话。顺便说一句，我接下来说的适用于表扬也适用于批评。让我稍作停顿。那个故事很有启发性，因为这类情况在我们很多人身上都发生过，并非我个人的特例。不过，在激进坦诚的语境下，表扬比批评更为重要。激进坦诚不应只是上司对员工的批评。它应该始于征求反馈，包含更多的表扬和批评，但切记不要给人留下“胡说八道”的印象。（00:15:31）所以，总之，我认为在这些即兴的两分钟管理对话中，保持谦逊至关重要。对我来说，我称之为坦诚而非真相，因为如果我走进房间说"莱尼，我要告诉你真相"，那就等于暗示自己通神，而对方一无所知。这不是激进坦诚的本质。这是一场对话，不是独白。因此，坦诚意味着我会说明自己对情况的理解，同时也好奇对方如何看待对话。所以你要保持谦逊，承认自己可能错了，这完全没关系。全知并非激进坦诚的必要条件，谢天谢地。所以要保持谦逊，表明自己想提供帮助。要记住对话内容，并明确告诉对方你这样做是为了帮助他们。（00:16:25）你不是想控制对方或打击他们之类的。你告诉他们是因为关心他们。所以要立即开始对话，最好是当场进行。我知道我说的这些并非绝对，但通常来说，如果我告诉自己和莱尼"等更好的时机再说"，那其实就是永远不说了。所以除非你情绪过于激动会说得很糟糕，或者对方情绪激动听不进去，否则就立刻行动。（00:17:16）还有一点，以前我主张当面进行对话，现在我建议同步对话，并推荐使用电话而非视频。芝加哥大学和其他机构的研究表明，面部表情和肢体语言的信息量远超实际表达，尤其是在电脑屏幕上的小方框里。但现实生活中可能也是如此，比如电话可能是我们有史以来最棒的沟通工具之一，因为通话时你只需专注于对方的话语，而这正是你此刻最想做的。所以一定要确保对话同步进行。
接下来你要做的是评估反馈效果如何。（00:18:15）：我稍后会详细讲解这个问题。但如果你通过邮件或短信进行反馈，就无法准确判断效果如何。Slack平台更是反馈沟通的灾难现场。我曾指导过一个总是在Slack上不断给出反馈的人，最后我实在忍无可忍，决定不再继续指导他。我当时说：“如果你继续犯这种错误，我没法做你的教练。”所以千万别这样做。花点时间拿起电话直接沟通吧。回想一下我小时候看到的AT&T广告——主动接触他人。你要表现出关怀之情。（00:18:52）：总结一下，要保持谦逊、提供真诚帮助、立即行动。最好能当面沟通，至少也要保持同步交流。如果无法当面交流，就要做到公开表扬、私下批评，同时避免针对对方性格进行褒贬。若想记住这些要点，可以用“HHIIPPP”来记忆：两个H、两个I，三个P（具体数量可灵活调整）。
（00:19:21）：再重点讲一下关于性格评价的部分。记住，无论是表扬还是批评，都要结合具体情境、观察结果和后续行动。比如在会议上，如果你每隔三句话就说“嗯”，结果让人觉得你很笨拙，后续建议去找演讲教练。同样在会议中，如果你能同时提出正反论点，就会赢得信任，接下来要多这样做。可以简称为“CORE”，也可理解为“核心原则”。我之前曾用“CORN”，但有人反馈说CORN在TikTok上是色情内容的缩写，所以现在改用“CORE”了，简称为“核心要点”。

turns.en: Because ruinous empathy creates this false harmony, which is really bad. So here's my ruinous empathy story. I had just hired this guy, we'll call him Bob, and I liked Bob a lot. He was smart, he was charming, he was funny. He would do stuff like we're at a manager offsite playing one of those endless get to know you games. And everybody was getting more and more and more stressed out. So start up, we've got a lot going on. And Bob was the guy who had the courage to raise his hand and to say, "I can tell everyone is getting stressed. I want to get to know all of you. I've got an idea. It'll help us do that and it'll be really fast." (00:21:41): Whatever his idea was, if it was really fast, we were down with it. And Bob says, "Let's just go around the table and confess what candy our parents used when potty training us." Really weird but really fast. And then for the next 10 months, every time there was a tense moment in a meeting, Bob would whip out just the right piece of candy for the right person at the right moment. And we all remember that was the weirder thing. Like Hershey Kisses right here. That was what my parents used to potty train me. (00:22:16): And so Bob was quirky, but he brought a little levity to the office. Everybody kind of loved working with Bob. There was one problem with Bob. He was doing terrible work. He would hand stuff into me and there was shame in his eyes. He kind of knew it wasn't good enough. He was very creative, but riddled with sloppy mistakes. And I would say something to Bob along the lines of, "Oh Bob, this is such a great start. You're so awesome. We all love working with you. Maybe you can make it just a little bit better." So let's pause for a moment. Why did I say such a banal thing to Bob? I think part of the problem was that I liked Bob and I really didn't want to hurt his feelings. (00:23:05): So that was the ruinous empathy part of why I said that. But also part of the problem was something more insidious, a little bit of manipulative insincerity, because Bob was popular and Bob was also sensitive kind of. And there was part of me that was afraid if I told Bob in no uncertain terms that his work wasn't nearly good enough, he would get upset. He might even start to cry and then everybody would think I was a big, you know what? So the part of me that was worried about my reputation as a leader, that was the manipulative insincerity part, the part of me that was worried about Bob's feelings, that was the ruinous empathy part. And this went on for 10 months, 10 long months, and I was so puzzled the whole time I couldn't understand what was going on. I learned much later that one of the issues perhaps was that Bob was smoking pot in the bathroom three times a day, which maybe explained all that candy that he had at all times. (00:24:11): But I didn't know any of that at the time. All I knew is that Bob was consistently doing bad work, but I wasn't really dealing with it. And eventually the inevitable happened. I realized that if I didn't fire Bob, I was going to lose all my best performers because not only had it been unfair to Bob not to tell him, I also had been unfair to everyone on the team. And they were frustrated. Their deliverables were late because his deliverables were late. They weren't able to do their best work because they were having to spend so much time redoing his work. (00:24:46): And the people who were best at their jobs were going to quit because they wanted to be able to do their best work. They were going to go to a different company where they could do their best work. And so I sat down to have a conversation with Bob that I should have begun frankly 10 months previously. And when I finished explaining to him where things stood, he kind of pushed his chair back from the table. He looked me right in the eye and he said, "Why didn't you tell me?" And as that question was going around in my head with no good answer, he looked at me again and he said, "Why didn't anyone tell me? I thought you all cared about me." And now I realized that by not telling Bob, thinking I was being so nice, I'm having to fire him as a result. Not so nice after all. But it was too late to say Bob because at this point even he agreed he should go because his reputation on the team was just shot. (00:25:46): All I could do in the moment was make myself a very solemn promise that I would never make that mistake again, and that I would do everything in my power to help other people avoid making that mistake. It was so painful. It was painful for me. It was painful for Bob, much more painful for Bob actually, and it was bad for the whole team and it was bad for our investors. We weren't getting results because of my ruinous empathy and ruinous empathy slash manipulative insincerity. It's much harder to admit the manipulative insincerity part. And that is really why I'm here talking to you because I want all of your listeners to avoid making that mistake because it's the most painful and the most common mistake that I think leaders and not just leaders, I mean all of us make this mistake in all of our relationships.

由于毁灭性的共情会制造出虚假的和谐，这实在是件坏事。所以让我讲讲我与毁灭性共情的故事。我刚招来一个叫鲍勃的员工，我很喜欢他。他聪明、迷人、风趣。有一回，我们参加管理层的户外活动，要玩那种没完没了的破冰游戏。每个人都越来越紧张。这时鲍勃挺身而出，说道："我看大家都越来越紧张了。我想认识你们所有人。有个主意，能快速达成目标。"（00:21:41）不管他的主意有多"快速"，我们都愿意尝试。鲍勃提议："咱们来轮流说父母训练我们上厕所时用的糖果。"听起来怪怪的，但确实很快就达成了目标。接下来的10个月里，每次会议出现紧张时刻，鲍勃总能精准地拿出合适的糖果给合适的人。我们都记得，那是最奇怪的时刻。比如赫尔希巧克力吻糖果——这就是我父母用来训练我上厕所的糖果。（00:22:16）鲍勃固然古怪，但他给办公室带来了轻松氛围。大家都喜欢和他共事。但鲍勃有个问题——他工作质量太差了。他交给我的东西，眼里都写着羞愧。他知道自己的工作不够好，但又极具创造力却满是低级错误。我会对鲍勃说类似"鲍勃，这真是个好的开始。你太棒了。我们都喜欢和你一起工作。或许你能再完善一下。"这样的话。暂停一下，我为什么要说这种陈词滥调？部分原因是我喜欢鲍勃，不想伤害他的感情。（00:23:05）这就是毁灭性共情的根源。但更深层的问题是操纵性虚伪。鲍勃很受欢迎，又很敏感。我担心如果直言他的工作不达标，他会生气，甚至哭出来，让大家觉得我是个混蛋。出于对领导声誉的担忧，这就是操纵性虚伪；出于对鲍勃感情的顾虑，这就是毁灭性共情。这种情况持续了10个月，漫长的10个月。我始终困惑不已，完全不明白发生了什么。后来才知道，鲍勃每天三次在洗手间吸大麻，这或许能解释他为什么总有糖果。（00:24:11）但当时我并不知道这些。我只知道鲍勃工作质量始终不达标，而我却没有采取有效措施。最终不可避免的结果是，我意识到如果不解雇鲍勃，就会失去所有优秀员工。因为既对鲍勃不公平，又对团队不公平。大家沮丧不已，交付成果延迟，因为鲍勃的任务总是延迟。优秀员工会离职，因为他们想专心做好本职工作。
于是，我坐下来与鲍勃进行了一次对话——这场对话本应在十个月前就坦诚开启的。当我向他解释现状时，他猛地将椅子从桌旁推开。他直直地盯着我，质问道：“你为什么不早告诉我？”面对这个问题，我脑海中反复思索却找不到合适的答案。他再次审视着我，继续追问：“为什么没人告诉我？我以为你们都关心我。”此刻我才意识到，出于所谓的善意，没有告诉鲍勃真相，最终导致我不得不解雇他。所谓善意，实则不善。然而事已至此，已无回头之路。

（00:25:46）那一刻，我只得郑重承诺，今后绝不再犯同样的错误，并竭尽全力帮助他人避免重蹈覆辙。这段经历异常痛苦——不仅于我于鲍勃，更波及整个团队和投资者。正是因我那致命的同理心与伪善的操纵术，我们错失了应有的成果。承认后者尤为艰难。正因如此，我今日站在这里向诸位讲述，希望所有听众都能汲取教训。这是领导者乃至所有人，在人际交往中最易犯却又最令人心碎的错误。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that this also gives an example of the impact of getting better at this point of you'll lose not just the people that are not necessarily great, but also other high performers on the team because they're seeing people slip through the cracks that aren't amazing. And if you're not practicing this early, your team basically becomes not high performing.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这段话还举了一个例子，说明了在某个阶段如果不能提升能力会带来怎样的影响——你不仅会失去那些表现不佳的人，还会失去团队中其他表现出色的人，因为他们会发现有能力不足的人被忽视了。如果你不尽早实践这种方法，整个团队的表现就会变得不佳。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. You're going to lose your top performers. And I think very often people are afraid to tell someone on their team when their work isn't good enough because they're afraid of losing them. But that's not a good reason. You should be helping this person to improve. This person deserves to have a job where they can excel and you either help them excel on this team or you help them find a different job where they can excel, because everyone can do great work somewhere. And Bob could have done great work. Maybe I would've helped him keep it to the weekends because he's very creative and very smart, but the floppy mistakes just got in the way of his ability to do his best work.
turns.zh: 是的，确实如此。你会失去顶尖人才。我认为很多人常常因为害怕失去团队成员而不敢指出他们的不足，但这并不是个好理由。你应该帮助他们提升。这些人理应在能充分施展才能的岗位上工作——要么帮助他们在现有团队中做到最好，要么帮他们找到能发挥潜力的新岗位，毕竟每个人都能在某个地方做出出色的工作。鲍勃本可以有所作为的。或许我本可以建议他把精力集中在周末，因为他极具创造力且才华横溢，但那些粗心的错误阻碍了他发挥最佳水平。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So following that thread, I imagine the reason you didn't tell him early, and most people don't do this well, is many people are, you can maybe call them people pleasers. I'm a recovering people pleaser, I'll say. It's just hard to give people hard feedback. You want people to like you. It's not a natural state for a lot of people. What do you find helps people get over this kind of need to be liked as a leader and helps them be more candid?
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，我猜你没有早点告知他的原因——多数人做得不好的地方在于，他们可能属于讨好型人格。我自己也在慢慢改掉这个毛病。给人提出批评意见实在太难了。人们总希望得到别人的认可，这对很多人来说并非天性作为领导者，你如何克服这种被认可的需求，变得更加坦诚？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: I think that one of the things that was helpful for me anyway, so you can tell me if it's helpful for you, was realizing that my job was not to be liked. My job was to care about other people and to get out of my own head and to become others focused is what helped me kind of let go of the need to be liked. I think that also as a woman, I think there was something extra, as my teenage children would say, there was something extra for me because the sort of likability- competence bias that a lot of women face pushed me, especially early in my career, in the wrong direction on challenge directly. (00:29:04): And it made it much harder for me to, because often I would say something and I would say it even more gently than my colleagues who were men, but people would say, "Ah, Kim is a real whatever." And they weren't saying, Kim is obnoxious. I was being unjustly accused of obnoxious aggression and it wasn't obnoxious or they were accusing me of being bossy or or abrasive or whatever. And it's really hard. I would also say when it comes to eliciting feedback, it's really important to be open to it and it's really important to separate the wheat from the chaff from the feedback you're getting.
turns.zh: 对我来说，关键在于意识到我的职责不是被喜欢，而是关心他人，摆脱自我中心，关注他人。这帮助我放下了被认可的需求。作为女性，我觉得还有额外的挑战——用我十几岁孩子的说法，就是额外的压力。很多女性面临的"可爱度与能力偏见"让我在职业生涯初期误入歧途。（00:29:04）当我提出批评时，即便比男性同事更委婉，人们还是会说：“啊，这位金女士真是无理取闹。”他们不是在说我讨人厌，而是指责我强势、粗鲁之类的。这真的很让人难受。另外，在获取反馈时，保持开放心态，区分有用的和无用的意见也很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So in this example of Bob, say you were to do it now, what would you do differently other than give him feedback earlier? Is there something you've learned about just how you would've phrased it or approached it?
turns.zh: 以鲍勃为例，如果你现在要处理这个问题，有什么不同之处吗？你有没有总结出如何更巧妙地表达或处理问题？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: I think probably what I would do, and I would love to hear what you would've said to Bob too, I certainly don't have all the answers, but probably what I would've said is let's go back to the first time Bob handed work into me with shame in his eyes. I would've said, "Bob, maybe I'm misinterpreting the expression on your face, but it looks to me like you are not happy with this. What's going on?" And so I would've asked him to diagnose it himself and I want to pause on that because that can be very risky. He might have said to me, "I think this is awesome. This is my best work," and now I've kind of made my job of giving him feedback a little bit harder. So it's not always the right thing to ask questions, but I would've tried to ask it before I had examined the work when I noticed that he looked uncomfortable himself. (00:30:47): And I think also another thing I've learned about noticing, I said earlier that there's a lot of evidence that we often misinterpret each other's facial expressions and body language. So I would've tried to say that with some humility, it seems like you're not, maybe I'm wrong, but you don't look to me like you're happy with this. And I would've given him an opportunity to say, "Yeah, maybe I need to do it again." Let's imagine though that he said, "Oh no, it's awesome. It's ready." So then I get it and I look at it. I would have not been shy about pointing out very specifically every problem that I saw in that piece of work, every single one. Sometimes it can be tempting when you're giving someone feedback to say, "Oh, there's a number of careless mistakes here. Can you go back and look at it again," and the person will notice a few of them and then you got to go, sometimes it's useful to show someone a pattern. (00:31:53): All of the careless mistakes, especially if someone is defensive or if you think they're likely to be defensive, if you think they're likely to do to you what I did to my boss, oh no, everything's fine. It's no big deal. You need to move out on the challenge directly dimension. You need to be prepared to keep going until you have communicated with a person. And that was really the problem with Bob. He probably would not have started to cry. I think my fear around his tears was probably more about my fear than what was actually likely to happen. But I think we do fear someone else getting upset more often than they actually get upset. We have kind of a negativity bias when it comes to part of the reason why we're reluctant to give feedback.
turns.zh:
我觉得我可能会这么做，我也很想听听你会对鲍勃说什么。我当然没有所有的答案，但我可能会说的是，让我们回到鲍勃第一次把作业交给我时，他眼中带着羞愧的时候。我会说：“鲍勃，也许我误解了你的表情，但在我看来你对这份作业不满意。怎么回事？”然后我会让他自己诊断问题所在——这里要稍作停顿，因为这可能很冒险。他可能会对我说：“我觉得这太棒了。这是我最出色的作品。”而现在我却让给他反馈的工作变得更难了。所以提问并不总是正确的做法，但我会试着在检查作品之前就提问，当我注意到他自己看起来很不自在的时候。（00:30:47）  
另外，我学到的关于观察的另一点是，我之前说过有很多证据表明我们经常误解彼此的面部表情和肢体语言。所以我会试着谦虚地说，看起来你不开心，也许我错了，但你看起来并不开心。然后我会给他一个机会说：“是的，也许我需要再做一遍。” 但假设他说：“哦，不，这太棒了。已经完成了。” 那么我拿到作业后，会非常具体地指出我看到的每一个问题。有时候，当你给别人反馈时，可能会想说：“哦，这里有几个粗心错误。你能再检查一遍吗？”对方会注意到几个错误，然后你就得结束了。有时候向对方展示一个模式会更有用。（00:31:53）  
所有这些粗心错误，尤其是如果对方很防御，或者你认为他们可能会防御，比如你认为他们会像我对我老板那样，哦，不，一切都好。你需要直接面对挑战。你需要准备好继续下去，直到你和对方沟通完毕。而这正是鲍勃的问题所在。他可能不会开始哭。我认为我对他流泪的恐惧更多是出于自己的担忧，而不是实际可能发生的情况。但我们确实比实际情况更害怕别人生气。谈到反馈时，我们有一种消极偏见，这也是我们不愿意给予反馈的部分原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think to your point, that we want to be liked, like you said, that you should get over that. I think that's obviously very hard just to be like, "Nah, I'm not going to worry about that." But I think your point is really important that you'll be liked later if you don't do the hard thing now. It'll only get worse if you just let it continue happening.
turns.zh: 而我认为你提到的观点很重要，就是我们希望被喜欢，正如你所说，你应该克服这种心理。我认为这显然很难做到，直接说“不，我才不在乎呢。”但我认为你的观点很重要，如果你现在不做艰难的事，以后你会被喜欢的。如果你任由事情继续发展，只会变得更糟。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: And I think also for me to say to myself going into that conversation, it's more important for me to demonstrate care, that I care about Bob than it is for Bob to like me, and if I demonstrate that I care about Bob, then I'm going to do the right thing that will ultimately create the conditions for a good relationship with Bob. Me pulling my punches did not create the conditions for a good relationship with Bob.
turns.zh: 而我认为对我自己来说，进入那次对话前，我要告诉自己，表现出关心比让鲍勃喜欢我更重要。如果我表现出关心鲍勃，那么我就会做正确的事，最终为与鲍勃建立良好的关系创造条件。而我退缩不做反馈并没有为与鲍勃建立良好的关系创造条件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I actually did that and I learned this from a manager of mine is just almost work backwards from ask them, what do you want to achieve in your career? Where do you want to go in this company and make sure they know you know what they want, and then basically work backwards from to get there. Here's the things you need to get, and here's the thing you did recently that isn't necessarily on the track and here's what we should be working on if you want to get to the skull that you have.
turns.zh: 实际上，我确实这么做过。我从一位上司那里学到的，就是先反向推导——先问他们：你职业生涯的目标是什么？你想在公司里达到什么样的位置？确保他们知道你清楚他们的期望，然后再反向规划达成目标的路径。首先列出你需要获得的条件，再回顾你最近做过的与目标不符的事项，最后制定实现目标的行动计划。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yeah, I think one of the really important things that all managers can do for their direct reports to show that they care is to have real meaningful career conversations, where you talk about their life story, sort of their past, whatever part of it they're comfortable talking to you about so that you understand what motivates them at work. And I would have three separate 45 minute conversations, so one about their past, one about their future, their dreams for the future, and it's not just the next couple of years. It's like imagine at the height of your career you have everything you want. What does it look like? And give me three or four different pictures of that because very few of us know what we want to do when we grow up. (00:34:40): Then the third conversation is to sort of sit down with your director report and come up with a career action plan. So given what motivates you and where you want to go, what are the skills that it would be useful for you to develop so that you can get where you want to go and who can I introduce you to? What are the educational opportunities? Can we tweak your job so that you're gaining those skills so you're at least taking a step in the direction of your dreams, even if you're not there yet?
turns.zh:
是的，我认为所有管理者能为直接下属做的最重要的事，就是通过真正有意义的职业对话来展现他们的关怀。在对话中，你要倾听他们的生活故事，了解他们的过去——只要他们愿意与你分享这部分——这样你就能理解他们的工作动力。为了更深入地理解他们的职业追求，我会进行三次45分钟的深度对话：一次探讨他们的过去，一次畅想他们的未来，还有一次构想理想中的职业蓝图。（00:34:40）  
第三次对话是与下属共同制定职业行动计划。基于他们的动机和职业目标，确定需要培养的技能，介绍可利用的教育资源，调整工作内容以助力他们获取所需技能，即便尚未达成目标，也能沿着梦想之路迈出坚实一步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I have a post about this. I'll link to in the show notes that gives people a guide to having these conversations, and there's a spreadsheet I share with people like, here's an action plan you can come up with your teammate and here's what you're going to work on these next six months.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我写过一篇关于这个主题的文章，会在节目笔记中附上链接，里面有指导如何开展这些对话的指南，还有我分享的电子表格，供团队成员制定未来六个月的行动计划。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Did you read the book When they Win, You Win by Russ Laraway?
turns.zh: 你读过拉塞尔·拉拉韦的《当他们赢了，你就赢了》这本书吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 没有。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Oh, he has a hundred pages on career conversations and he's also built sort of some tools that help people. So check that out.
turns.zh: 哦，他有整整一百页讲职业对话的内容，还开发了一些工具帮助人们。所以你可以去看看。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's called When You Win... When They Win, You Win.
turns.zh: 书名叫《当他们赢了……当你赢了，大家都赢了》。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: When They Win, You Win.
turns.zh: 《当他们赢了……当你赢了，大家都赢了》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yes, by Russ Laraway, he and I worked together at Google and then we started a company together.
turns.zh: 是的，作者是拉塞尔·拉拉韦，我和他曾在谷歌共事过，后来还一起创办了公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh wow. Okay, cool. We'll link to them in the show notes. Maybe I'll get him on the podcast too. Great.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。好的，太棒了。我们会把相关信息放在节目笔记里，或许还能邀请他上播客。太好了。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yeah, he'd be great.
turns.zh: 对，他会很棒的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so we've been chatting about ways individually to get better at some of these skills. Another area that I think people struggle with is the company culture often isn't welcoming of direct feedback. So there's a question, so you probably saw this on Twitter. I asked people, what should I ask you? And a lot of people came in with a lot of questions and there's one that came in from Pete, so I'm just going to read it along these lines. So this question is just how do you practice being radically candid in a culture? And most cultures are like this where people aren't ready for direct feedback. Since company culture is often closer to ruinous empathy and being radically candid is more of a long-term good than a short-term good. You could potentially risk retention with your employees if you're too direct with them. So how do you think about finding this balance of being candid but not pissing people off, or do you just hire people that are open and ready for direct feedback and that's kind of how you solve that problem?
turns.zh: 好的，我们之前一直在讨论如何通过个人努力提升某些技能。还有一个领域我觉得大家比较头疼，那就是公司文化往往不欢迎直接反馈。所以这里有个问题，你们可能在推特上看到过。我问大家：我该问你们什么？很多人提了不少问题，其中有来自皮特的一个问题，我现在就来照着念一下。问题是，在这种不愿接受直接反馈的文化中，如何践行彻底坦诚？大多数公司文化都是这样的，人们还没准备好接受直接反馈。毕竟公司文化往往更倾向于无原则的同情，而彻底坦诚更多是长期的益处而非短期的利好。如果你对员工太直接，可能会影响员工留存率。那么，如何在保持坦诚的同时，又不惹人反感呢？或者你是否应该直接招募那些乐于接受直接反馈、思想开放的人？这样就能轻松解决这个问题了。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: I don't think you can only hire people who are open and ready for direct feedback because it's hard for all of us. I just want to acknowledge that, it's hard for me. I mean, I wrote the book, I believe in it to my core and sometimes it's still hard for me. It's hard for me to hear it and it's hard for me to deliver it. This is a really difficult thing to do. The good thing about that two by two is it makes it look easy, which is useful, but it's not easy. So anyway, I think there are, to answer Pete's question, I think there are a few things that can help. There's really an order of operations to radical candor, and if you begin with soliciting criticism, then you take the first and most important step to improving your relationship with that person enough that it becomes easier for you to give it as well as to get it. (00:37:35): So I want to leave folks with some sort of steps on how to solicit feedback, and this is true, especially if you're a boss, but it's true in all your relationships. You can use this at home as well. So if you say, "Do you have any feedback for me?" You're wasting your breath. The other person's going to say, "Oh no, everything's fine." turns.zh: 绝不这样做。我的意思是，有些人确实不喜欢被逼到墙角。所以如果我意识到自己正在给对方施加一种残酷又不寻常的惩罚，我会说：“听着，你知道我并不完美。我知道自己并不完美。下次见面时，我希望你能留意到一些东西，注意到一些细节。最重要的是，当我犯错时，你能及时指出，这比任何其他帮助都更有意义。”事实上，英特尔前首席执行官安迪·格罗夫曾透露，他在一对一会议结束时常对员工说：“还有一件事。”他向我解释说，这句话是英特尔内部的暗号，意思是“这才是最重要的事”。当时我在苹果工作，我问：“哦，你是从史蒂夫·乔布斯那里学来的吗？”（00:42:47）乔布斯每次发布新产品时也常用这句话：“就再说一件事——iPad。” 安迪立刻变得很不高兴，生气地说：“不，我们都是从《警探科伦坡》里学来的。” 你可以从任何地方获取灵感。所以你要确保让对方知道你真的在乎他们的意见，当他们给你这种批评性的反馈时，你会给予奖励。但这还不是终点。提出这个问题只是第一步。关于你的问题，坏消息是，无论你怎么绞尽脑汁想问题，问得多好，对方还是会感到不自在。没有所谓的情感麻醉剂。这就是为什么我不相信照本宣科。人们以为只要说出那些魔法词句，比如“门就会打开”，但事实并非如此。这是一个互动的过程。所以你要做好迎接这种不自在的准备。唯一的出路就是直面它。迎接不自在最简单的方法就是闭上嘴巴，数到六。（00:43:59）你刚才只数到三，而且眼睛都瞪大了。

It doesn't mean you're a lesser mortal or that you're shut down the feedback. All it means is that you're human. And that's all part of this. You want to figure out how to manage your natural defensive reaction to critical feedback, which you're probably going to have. The simplest tactic I can offer folks there is to think of some follow-up questions. (00:44:56): So at breakfast, my daughter not too long ago said to me, "Mom, I wish you weren't the Radical Candor lady." And immediately this wave of parental guilt washed over me and I thought, ah, I'm spending too much time at work. She wants more of my time. I shouldn't be traveling so much. But then I thought, well, I should ask her, make sure I understood. I'm jumping to conclusions here. I'm not listening with the intent to understand. So I asked a follow-up question. I said, "Well, who do you wish I were?" And she said, "I wish you were the lady who minded her own business," so I could go spend a little more time at work as far as she was concerned. So you want to make sure you really understand what a person is telling you. And once you feel certain that you really do understand and that you've been open to it, the last and most important step is to reward the candor. (00:45:46): A person takes a huge risk, especially if this person is your employee. A person takes a huge risk to give you critical feedback. And if you do not reward that risk richly, you're never going to get any feedback again. So if you agree with the feedback, fix the problem and make your listening tangible, be loud. So-and-so told me that the tea in the break room is terrible, and now we have thirty-five different kinds of tea. Thank you for telling me. And that can demonstrate to people that they're not wasting their breath to come to you. That if you become aware of a problem, you'll fix it. (00:47:10): And so what you want to do is you want to look for that five or 10% of whatever the person said that you can agree with, and you want to give voice to that. And then what you want to do is you want to say, "As for the rest of it, I want to think about it and get back to you." And then you've got to get back to them. You got to offer a respectful explanation of why you disagree.
