turns.zh: 别只说谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Especially if you disagree, which is a really interesting nuance of this. I had Jules Walter on the podcast. I always think of him when I think of getting feedback. He shared this advice. When you get feedback, just be so appreciative so that people keep giving me just like, "Thank you so much for that feedback." The way he phrases it. Even if you're melting inside and really hate this feedback, just like, "thank you, I really appreciate it." But I think your nuance there is really key is if you do disagree, I really like this tip of just like, let me think about this element of it and then actually follow up.
turns.zh: 特别是当你不同意意见时，这是一个非常有趣的细微之处。我曾邀请朱尔斯·沃尔特上节目。每当我想到获取反馈时，总会想起他。他分享了这样一个建议：当收到反馈时，要表现出极大的感激，这样人们会继续给予反馈。比如“非常感谢你的反馈”。他表达的方式。即使你内心其实很生气、很讨厌这些反馈，也要说“谢谢，我真的很感激”。但我认为关键的细微之处在于，如果你确实不同意，你可以先想一想其中的要点，然后再跟进。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Even if you're melting inside, if you say thank you and you're melting inside, I mean maybe it's a terrible actor, but usually people know. And that's why I say it's not enough to say thank you. You got to fix the problem and then show what you did to fix the problem and get more feedback. Did I over-correct? Did I under-correct. And if you disagree, you got to say that you disagree, but you got to say, so respectfully.
turns.zh: 即便你内心如火般焦急，就算你说了声“谢谢”却仍心潮澎湃，我想这或许说明对方演技实在糟糕，但通常人们都能察觉。因此，我认为光是说声“谢谢”远远不够。你必须解决问题，然后展示改进之处，并收集更多反馈。改进过度了？改进不足了？若有异议，必须坦诚相告，但要保持尊重。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As a leader, this sounds like a lot of work to be doing every week. If you have a one-on-one following up correcting things. Is there anything you'd recommend there? Or is it just, this is really important, you got to make time.
turns.zh: 作为领导者，每周开展这样的追踪纠错工作听起来确实费力。如果你要进行一对一的跟进纠错，那是否还有其他建议？或者说，这件事至关重要，你必须挤出时间来。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: It's not as much work as failing to do this as we saw from the Bob story. So I think that the important thing that I have found is that this is part of why it's so important to do it immediately. It's important for the other person, but it's also important for you. If you're doing this in a one-on-one, which you should be having anyway. So you're saving some time in a one-on-one. So it's not adding time necessarily to your day. And when you hear about problems, you should fix them. Yes, it takes time, but that is your job. And when you disagree with something, you can disagree in your next regularly scheduled one-on-one. So I'm not talking about adding meetings to your calendar, so it doesn't actually take more time. I have found that in fact, it saves tremendous amounts of time, but it does take emotional discipline. (00:51:52): And I think it also requires you, especially when it comes to giving it, which we talked about before, where the humble, helpful, those are impromptu two-minute conversations, giving the feedback that you should be having in between your meetings. In the um story, walk to my meeting with me, it didn't take any extra time for my boss to give me that feedback. She had to walk to her meeting anyway, and I had to go in the same direction. So it didn't even take extra time from me. But it is, I think one of the most common reasons why people don't do this in addition to fear of retaliation and just sort of existential dread, which are both factors, which hopefully we've helped alleviate, but is that you're scheduled back to back to back and you don't have those two minutes in between meetings. (00:52:42): And that's why I think it's important either to schedule slack time in your calendar, make your 30 minute meetings, 25 minute meetings, make your hour-long meetings, 50 minute meetings, maybe give yourself a few breaks in the day. But if it's not possible, and often it was not possible for me in my career to sort of schedule my time that way, I just decided that these moments of management were more important than being on time to my next meeting. And so I was just late sometimes. So I wish I had a better answer than either control your time, which is really annoying advice because it's impossible to follow or be willing to be late to your next meeting. But those were the things that I tried to do.
turns.zh: 相比鲍勃的故事中那种未能及时纠错的后果，这项工作所耗费的精力要少得多。所以我发现，最重要的是要立即行动。这不仅对对方有益，对自己也有益。若已开展一对一的绩效追踪（这本身就应该是常态），那么在一对一会议中就能节省时间。因此，这并不会额外占用你的时间。当听到问题时，就应该立即解决。是的，这需要时间，但这是你的职责。当存在分歧时，可以在下次定期一对一会议中提出异议。所以我不是说要在日程中增加会议，这实际上并不会增加时间负担。我发现这反而能节省大量时间，但这需要情感自律。（00:51:52）：我认为这也是人们不愿采取行动的最常见原因之一——除了害怕遭到报复和存在生存焦虑（这两个因素我们已帮助缓解），还在于日程安排过于紧凑，会议间隙没有两分钟时间进行反馈。（00:52:42）：因此，我认为要么在日程中安排缓冲时间，将30分钟会议缩短至25分钟，将一小时会议延长至50分钟，或许每天给自己几个休息时间。但若无法做到这些（在我的职业生涯中常遇此情况），我就决定这些管理时刻比准时参加下次会议更重要。因此我有时会迟到。所以我希望能给出更好的建议，但要么控制时间（这条建议实在令人厌烦，因为根本无法遵循），要么甘愿偶尔迟到。但这些都是我曾尝试过的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was super helpful. I think your point of just, if you're not making two minutes to do this thing now, it'll be a lot more time intensive later.
turns.zh: 这真是太有帮助了。我觉得你的观点很到位——如果你现在不抽出两分钟时间去做这件事，以后就会花费更多时间。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Oh yeah. It's stitch in time takes nine on all these two minute, and really it should be brushing and flossing. This is not like a root canal. These are like, this is relationship hygiene that you should be doing all the time.
turns.zh: 哦，对啊。这就像是亡羊补牢，事后亡羊补牢总比亡羊不补牢强。说真的，应该早点刷牙、用牙线。这可不是做根管治疗。这就像是人际关系的日常维护，你得时刻保持良好的人际关系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was just reading Charlie Munger's book and there's a quote that he references of just the classic, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.
turns.zh: 我刚在读查理·芒格的书，里面引用了一句古话——“防患于未然，胜于亡羊补牢”。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yes, absolutely.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Same idea. So we've talked about a leader getting feedback. What if you're the employee? Do you also recommend the same thing in the one-on-one, have an agenda item and ask this question? Or is there a different approach you'd recommend?
turns.zh: 道理是一样的。我们之前讨论了领导者如何获取反馈，那如果你是员工呢？你是否也会建议在一对一会议中加入类似议题，提出这个问题？还是说你有更推荐的处理方式？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: I think yes, if you're the employee, you should also be soliciting feedback on a regular basis from your boss. So there's sort of an order of operations you want to solicit at first, no matter who you are, it's the same up, down, and sideways, even though it feels very different, the order of operations is the same. So start by soliciting feedback. Then you want to give both praise and criticism. I think sometimes it feels like you're kissing up if you give your boss praise, but bosses need praise too. And if there are things that your boss does that you appreciate and you want your boss to do more of those things, praise is a better tool for that than criticism. When it comes time to offering your boss some critical feedback, you want to make sure, and by the way, this is also true when it comes time to give your employee critical feedback or your spouse or anybody else in your life, you want to be sure that you are prepared to gauge how it lands. (00:55:09): So you want to start in kind of a neutral place. You don't want to go to the outer edge of challenge directly because then you're going to wind up in obnoxious aggression. So if we go back to that story, my boss started, "You said um a lot, were you aware of it?" "Nah." That was my response. And then "I know this great speech coach, would you like an introduction?" "Nah," was my response. So she had to keep going out on that challenge directly. She didn't start out by saying, "When you say um I'm every third word, it makes you sound stupid." But she realized she had to go that far. So you want to keep going out if you think they're brushing you off. But if you find that your boss looks either sad or mad, that is your cue to move up on the care personally dimension. (00:55:51): And so to take a moment, and if you find your employee looks sad or mad, if they look sad, pause and say, "I feel like maybe I didn't say that in the best possible way. How could I have said it differently?" And so that means you're going up on the care personally, dimension, but you're not going the wrong way on challenge directly. I don't know about you Lenny, but if I say something to someone and they look sad, it's so tempting for me to try to pull the words back. "Oh no, it's no big deal. I didn't mean it," but it is a big deal, and I did mean it, that's why I just said it. And so if you go the wrong way on challenge directly, you wind up in ruinous empathy, and then you leave the person both sad and confused, so you make it worse. (00:56:34): So you want to take a beat to pay attention to the emotions in the moment, but not to go the wrong way on challenge directly. Same thing if they're mad, although if somebody's mad, that maybe is even harder. If somebody starts yelling at me, it's tempting for me either to start yelling back and wind up in obnoxious aggression or to crawl off to a self-protective, manipulative insincerity. And so instead, what I try to do is get curious, not furious, and why is this person so mad? So say like, Look, maybe I didn't say that in the right way, but this is an important issue and we need to resolve it.
turns.zh: 我认为是的，如果你是员工，你也应该定期向你的老板征求反馈意见。所以无论你是谁，征求反馈时都应该遵循一定的顺序——先上后下，再横向拓展，尽管感觉可能大不相同，但核心步骤是一样的。首先要征求反馈。然后要给予赞扬和批评。我认为有时候给老板赞扬会让人觉得你在拍马屁，但老板也需要被赞扬。如果有老板做的事情让你欣赏，并且希望他们能多做些类似的事，赞扬比批评更有效。当要给老板提出批评意见时，你必须确保自己准备好衡量对方的反应。（00:55:09）所以要从中立的角度入手，不要直接挑战对方，否则会显得过于冒犯。回到那个故事，我老板一开始问：“你老是嗯嗯嗯，是不是没意识到？”我回答：“没有啊。”然后她又说：“我认识一个很棒的演讲教练，要不要我介绍给你？”我还是回答：“不必。”所以她不得不继续直接挑战。她没有一开始就说：“你每隔三句话就嗯嗯嗯，显得很笨。”但她意识到必须走到那一步。所以如果你觉得对方在回避你的反馈，就要继续深入。但如果你发现老板看起来很伤心或生气，这就是你需要转向关怀维度的信号。（00:55:51）所以要暂停一下，如果员工看起来伤心或生气，要说：“我觉得我可能表达得不太好。我该怎么换种说法呢？”这样你在关怀维度上有所提升，同时又没有在挑战维度上走错路。我不知道你怎么想，莱尼，但如果我对别人说了什么，他们看起来很伤心，我就会忍不住想收回话：“哦没关系的，我不是故意的。”但这确实很重要，我确实是认真的，这就是我说出来的原因。如果你在挑战维度上走错路，就会陷入破坏性共情，让对方既伤心又困惑，情况只会更糟。（00:56:34）所以你要停下来，注意对方当下的情绪，但不要在挑战维度上走错路。同样，如果对方生气，更难处理了。如果有人对我大喊大叫，我很想反击或者退缩到自保、操纵的虚伪中。所以相反，我会保持好奇心，而不是愤怒，问自己：为什么这个人这么生气？比如说：“看，也许我的表达方式不对，但这是一个重要的问题，我们需要解决它。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This comes back to the point you made about when you're giving feedback to try to do it in person or on a phone call to do exactly what you're saying, to read them as you're giving this feedback and figure out which axis you want to go down.
turns.zh: 这又回到了你之前提到的观点——当你给出反馈时，无论是面对面还是通过电话，都要按照你所说的去做，在反馈时观察对方的反应，判断你应该在哪个维度上深入。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yeah, you want to gauge it. I mean, when we communicate with other people, we communicate on an emotional level and on an intellectual level at the same time. And if we ignore the emotional signals that are coming at us or say don't take it personally, then we're just not going to communicate very well.
turns.zh: 是的，你需要去感知这种影响。我的意思是，当我们与他人交流时，我们既在情感层面沟通，也在理智层面交流。如果我们忽视传递给我们的情感信号，或者说"别往心里去"，那我们的沟通效果就不会太好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these same lines, another question that came in is from a coach of yours that works I think for you or somehow with the program. She asked this question of many top leaders have very low self-awareness. They believe obnoxious aggression is the only way to give feedback, or they just ignore the problem and fire people with no feedback. Is there something you've learned about how to change their mind about this is the way to operate?
turns.zh: 基于同样的思路，还有一个问题来自于一位你的教练，我想她是为你工作的，或者与你的项目有关。她问道，许多高层领导自我意识很低。他们认为粗鲁的攻击性是提供反馈的唯一方式，或者他们干脆忽视问题，然后解雇员工却不给出反馈。对于如何改变他们的这种行为方式，你有没有什么心得？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yeah, I think the most important thing with leaders like that, that you can do is to explain to them the impact that they're having and to also show them that there is another way that is going to help them succeed. Very often the leaders who are low on the care personally dimension, they do care about their results and they do care about their own careers. And so when you sort of explain this to them in terms of enlightened self-interest, they tend to get better at it. And also, I mean there I can think of maybe one or two people I've worked with who are truly low on care, who truly don't care. Very often people are bad at showing they care, but they do actually care. And also sometimes there are leaders who think they're not supposed to care. And so unleashing that capacity that they innately have to care and telling them this is actually part of the job can make them a much better, more effective leader. But look, if someone is a psychopath and they truly don't care, they shouldn't be a manager. That's the solution.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为对于这类领导者，最重要的是向他们解释他们的行为所产生的影响，并向他们展示还有另一种方法可以帮助他们成功。很多在关怀他人维度得分较低的领导者，他们确实关心自己的业绩，也关心自己的职业生涯。所以当你从利己主义的角度向他们解释这一点时，他们往往会做得更好。此外，我能想到可能有那么一两个我合作过的领导者，他们真的很冷漠，真的不在乎别人的感受。很多时候，人们不善于表达自己的关怀，但他们实际上确实在乎。有时甚至有些领导者认为他们不应该关心别人。因此，释放他们天生就有的关怀能力，并告诉他们这实际上是工作的一部分，可以让他们成为更出色、更高效的领导者。但听着，如果有人是精神病患者，真的不在乎，那他们就不应该当经理。这才是解决之道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I totally get that one. So I really like that takeaway. Just basically show them the impact they're having because to your point, they want the company to succeed. They want their team to succeed. And if they're not realizing there's downsides to the way they're operating.
turns.zh: 我完全理解这个观点。所以我真的很喜欢这个启示。基本上就是向他们展示他们的影响，因为正如你所说，他们希望公司成功。他们希望团队成功。如果他们没有意识到自己的行为有负面影响。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: And they want themselves to succeed. That's why I say part of the problem with obnoxious aggression is that you harm other people, but it's also inefficient because when you act like that, people can't hear what you're saying, so you're wasting your breath.
turns.zh: 还有他们希望自己成功。这就是为什么我说粗鲁攻击性的部分问题在于，你会伤害他人，但这也很低效，因为当你这样做时，别人听不进你说的话，所以你在白费力气。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the way you show them that impact. Do you recommend interviewing people, getting stories, seeing, I don't know, how do you collect this impact so that they're like, oh, wow, I didn't realize this.
turns.zh: 而你向他们展示这种影响的方式。你建议采访人们、收集故事、观察等等，我不知道，你是如何收集这种影响的，让他们会说，哦，哇，我没有意识到这一点。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: I think that the best thing to do is, for me anyway, is I start by sharing stories from my career and stories when I was a jerk. I've acted like a jerk too, plenty of times, unfortunately. And I show the impact that I've had and then I ask them for a similar story. And usually sort of me holding up the mirror to myself is useful for them to be able to hold the mirror up to themselves to realize you want to help these people adopt a growth mindset around this stuff. I am not telling you that you're an asshole. I'm telling you that we all behave like assholes sometimes. And it's a big problem for us as well as for the people around us. And here's my story, when I acted like a jerk, what's yours? And people, that kind of self-awareness, sometimes people talk about inflicted insight like it's some kind of burden, but usually that kind of self-awareness makes people feel lighter. They're like, "Ah, now I know what's wrong and now I know what I can do about it."
turns.zh: 我觉得对我来说，最好的做法是先分享自己职业生涯中的故事，以及我曾表现得像个混蛋的时候。很不幸，我也经常这样做。我会展示自己行为带来的影响，然后请他们分享类似的经历。通常，让他们自我反省能帮助他们反思自己，从而意识到你想帮助这些人养成一种成长型思维模式。我不是说你是个混蛋，而是说我们都时常表现得像个混蛋。这对我们自己和身边的人来说都是个大问题。接下来是我的故事——当我表现得像个混蛋时，你的故事是什么？这种自我反省的能力，有时人们会把它视为一种负担，但通常这种自我觉察能让人感觉轻松许多。他们会说：“啊，现在我知道问题出在哪儿了，也知道该怎么改进了。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I've definitely noticed that about your stories. They always are you making the mistake, which I think is very disarming.
turns.zh: 是啊，我确实注意到你讲的故事总是自己犯错，这让我觉得很坦诚。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: We all make mistakes.
turns.zh: 我们都会犯错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Maybe the extreme of this obnoxious aggressiveness is Bridgewater. Their whole approach is like theirs.
turns.zh: 是啊，也许最极端的这种令人不快的攻击性就是桥水基金了。他们的整个管理方式就是这样。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Oh my gosh. Did you read the book The Fund?
turns.zh: 天哪。你读过《基金》这本书吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, not yet.
turns.zh: 没有，还没读。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: You must read it. It's all about Bridgewater. I always thought it was problematic. I had no idea just how problematic it is. Put that book in the show notes one of the best business books I've read in the last decade.
turns.zh: 你一定要读。这本书全是关于桥水基金的。我一直觉得它存在问题。真没想到问题如此严重。把这本书加到节目笔记里吧——这是我过去十年读过的最棒的商业书籍之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that is high praise. Yes, I will read that. And so I guess for people that aren't familiar, like Bridgewater, they encourage, they have a system called Dots where they tell people, you must give hard critical feedback after every meeting, publicly.
turns.zh: 哇，这评价可真高了。好的，我会读的。那么对于不熟悉桥水基金的人来说，他们鼓励员工使用一个叫“Dots”的系统，要求人们在每次会议后公开进行严厉的批评反馈。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Not after the meeting, in the meeting, publicly. And it's recorded on, it was, I think they changed it since, but it was recorded for posterity on video. And sometimes, in fact, true story, shortly after I left Google, I was approached to work at Bridgewater in a management capacity, not in an investment capacity. And so I called someone I knew who worked there and he said, "Let me give you an anecdote." He said, "The other day there was a meeting and there was a woman who in the meeting who had made a mistake and everybody just piled on. The criticism was very personal. There was no core about the criticism. It was like, these are your personality attributes that make you a useless human being. Kind of terrible feedback until she started to cry and the whole meeting was recorded and then they emailed a recording of the meeting out to the whole company, including all the people who were not in the meeting saying, this is an example of how to have..." So I would say that is deep, dark, obnoxious aggression. That is not radical candor. That is horrible.
turns.zh: 不是会后，而是会议期间公开进行。反馈会被录像记录下来（虽然后来他们改了政策）。我有个朋友在那里工作，他给我讲了个真实故事。离开谷歌不久后，有人找我去桥水基金担任管理职位，而不是投资职位。我打电话给认识的在那里工作的人，他说：“让我给你讲个小插曲。”他说：“前几天开会，有个女同事犯了错，大家都开始互相攻击。批评内容非常针对个人，而不是针对问题本身。比如说，‘你性格里有这些缺点，让你成了个没用的人。’这种糟糕透顶的反馈，直到她哭了出来。会议全程被录像了，然后他们把录像发给了全公司所有人，包括没参加会议的人，告诉大家这是如何进行批评的……” 所以我觉得这就是深层的、黑暗的、令人不快的攻击性。这不是激进的坦诚，而是可怕的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it's safe to say you're not a fan of that approach?
turns.zh: 所以可以说你不喜欢这种管理方式？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: No. In fact, I did an analysis of Dalio's book Principles and it's like a, I don't know, 3 or 400 page book. And there were I think four or five pages about caring about people. There's very low care personally.
turns.zh: 事实上，我分析了达利奥的《原则》这本书，整本书有三四百页，我记得其中只有四五页讲的是关怀他人。他个人对员工的关怀程度很低。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine many people see that, they see Elon, they see Steve Jobs, and the perception is they're very challenge directly people, they're not clearly care about you people, but they're very successful. What do you say to people that are like, but it works. Why wouldn't I be that if that's the way I want to do it?
turns.zh: 我觉得很多人看到达利奥、埃隆和乔布斯这些人，会觉得他们对下属要求很严厉，不怎么关心员工，但他们却非常成功。对于那些说“但这确实有效啊，为什么我不能这样做？”的人，你会怎么说？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Well, first of all, I would not put Steve Jobs in the same category as Ray Dalio and Elon Musk. I mean, Steve Jobs could be obnoxiously aggressive, but mostly I would say he built such good relationships with his direct reports that when he got cancer, Tim Cook offered to give him half his liver. And I don't know of a word to describe that other than love. These were real human relationships. When I worked at Apple, you could see Steve and Johnny talking. You could tell these people cared about each other. Now, radical candor gets measured not at the speaker's mouth, but at the listener's ear. And I think that Steve had built a team around him of people who didn't mind rather what other people would consider obnoxious aggression. But I think in the context of their relationship, it was understood as care. (01:05:03): I'll give you an example of that from my own career, not that I am comparing myself to Steve Jobs, I think I'm a much gentler person, but sometimes I develop relationships with people. And part of that relationship is that we push each other pretty hard. So there was a person who I had worked with for a long time, for many years. He had followed me from one company to another, and we were localizing a product and he kept conflating Slovakia and Slovenia, and I corrected him once. I corrected him twice the third time, I was like, did Slovakia, not Slovenia dumb ass. (01:05:44): And he started laughing, and that was fine in the context of our relationship, but I realized that the people around me, I was silencing them. They were like, "Oh my gosh, I don't want to make a mistake. Kim's going to call me a dumb ass." So I had to pause and say, "Look, I respect this person enormously, and I like this person enormously. We work very well together." And so I think that sometimes people have relationships with others and they have those relationships in public and other people misinterpret those relationships. (01:06:19): Steve Jobs was not perfect. He made all kinds of mistakes, but he was no Ray Dalio or Elon Musk, who I would say make far more and worse and more egregious mistakes. And I think you're raising a really important point. You're raising a point, which is that there's this false dichotomy. In fact, the new biography of Elon Musk falls into this category. I like Walter Isaacson's work a lot, but he falls prey to this in his biography of Elon Musk, which is there's this notion that we have to choose between being a total jerk but really competent or really nice but incompetent. And those are not our two choices. That's the whole point of radical candor is that there's this other way that works better and doesn't hurt people.
turns.zh:
首先，我不认为乔布斯和马斯克能归为同一类人。乔布斯可能有些让人不适的强势，但他和直接下属的关系非常好。比如他得癌症时，库克主动提出愿意捐出半个肝脏。这份情谊无法用言语形容，那是真挚的人情。苹果公司内部，你能看到乔布斯和乔尼交谈，看得出他们彼此关心。所谓的"激进坦诚"不是看说话者的态度，而是看听者的反应。乔布斯身边的团队成员并不介意别人眼中的"过分强势"，但在他们的关系中，这被视为关怀。
 (01:05:03): 我举个自己职业生涯中的例子——当然我不是在拿自己和乔布斯比，我觉得自己温和多了——但有时我和同事会建立深厚的关系。这种关系的一部分就是互相鞭策。有个和我共事多年的下属，跟着我从一家公司跳到另一家。我们在本地化产品时，他总把斯洛伐克和斯洛文尼亚搞混，我纠正了他一次，纠正了两次。第三次我忍无可忍，说，"斯洛伐克不是斯洛文尼亚，你个白痴！" 他笑了，在我们关系里这没问题。但我意识到周围的人都在压抑自己的声音，担心"天哪，我可不想犯错，金会说我是个白痴"。所以我不得不停下来，说："听着，我非常尊重和欣赏这个人。我们合作得很愉快。" 我觉得有时候人们建立关系，公开场合表现得亲密无间，却被外人误解。
 (01:06:19): 乔布斯并不完美，他犯过很多错，但他和达利奥、马斯克不一样。马斯克犯的错更多、更严重、更离谱。我觉得你提出了一个重要观点：人们常把两种极端对立起来。但新出的马斯克传记就犯了这个错误。我很欣赏沃尔特·艾萨克森的作品，但他在传记里陷入了这种二元论，认为要么做个十足混蛋但高效，要么心地善良但无能。其实这两者并非唯一选择。激进坦诚的核心观点是，存在第三种更有效、更人性化的相处方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's the key takeaway there is you can be even more successful if you lean into the care deeply. In theory, they could have gotten more out of their people if they made it clear they really care about them.
turns.zh: 我认为关键在于，如果你能更真诚地关怀他人，你会取得更大的成功。从理论上讲，如果领导者能让员工感受到自己真正关心他们，他们本可以从员工身上获得更多价值。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: And there's plenty of counter examples of incredibly successful people who are very caring leaders, and it's not as much fun to tell stories about that. And so we don't as often.
turns.zh: 然而现实中也有很多成功人士是善于关怀他人的领导者，但讲述这类故事并不那么有趣，所以我们不常提及。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along the same lines, there's someone that you worked with that suggested I ask you about investing in your authentic leadership style, Melissa Tan. I don't know if you remember her.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 好的，很棒。她曾与你共事过，她建议我向你请教如何投资于真实的领导力风格，梅丽莎·谭。我不知道你是否还记得她。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. And she was on the podcast in the past, and she just said how when she met you, she was a very people-pleasery person and just wanted to be like, and you helped her develop her natural leadership style. Can you just talk about what you suggest to people to figure this out and how to find that for yourself?
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: I mean, I wonder what Melissa would say, but my memory of conversations with her, and this is an issue that I talk about a lot because a people pleaser too. I grew up in the South and I'm a woman. I was not brought up to challenge directly. That was not part of the culture that I was brought up in. I was brought up to be polite but also brought up to be kind. And for me, the thing that is most important to hang on to is that fundamental kindness and to realize that it's actually unkind not to say the thing. And so that is part of the reason why I encourage people. I tell the Bob story so often and I encourage other leaders who I work with to think about what their Bob story is that you realize it's not nice in the long run. (01:09:00): It's unkind in the long run, not to tell someone if they're making a mistake. There's nothing nice about that in the long run. And so that I think at least for me, that's been helpful. And then another thing that is helpful is again, to get others focused, to focus not on pleasing people, but on doing the right thing for those people, on truly caring about those people more than you care about your own discomfort in the moment. And that is something that is easier for people to do than just to challenge directly. I think in many ways it's about what is getting in the way. That's why I call it ruinism. Empathy is a good thing, but sometimes empathy can paralyze at least me because I'm so acutely aware of how what I'm going to say might impact the other person, might hurt their feelings that I don't say it. (01:10:01): And so when I push myself to be, and you can call it compassionate candor if you like that better than radical candor. But when I push myself not to feel so acutely what I think the other person might feel, and by the way, I could be wrong about what I think the other person might often, they're like, it's no big deal. They're like, oh, thank you for letting me know. But when I can let go of that and think about the other person and what I care about and what they care about for their future, going back to your point, if you know that it's really important for someone to get promoted and they won't get promoted if they keep talking to people in a particular way, then you're focused on what they want. That is really helpful to move past that.
turns.zh: 嗯，我很好奇梅丽莎会怎么说，但我对与她交谈的记忆深刻——因为我自己也曾是个讨好型人格。我在南方长大，是个女性，从小被教育要保持礼貌，但又不能直接反驳别人。这不是我成长的文化所允许的。我被教导要礼貌待人，但更要善良。对我来说，最重要的是保持这种基本的善良，并意识到不说出真相实际上是不善良的。所以这就是我鼓励人们的原因。我经常讲鲍勃的故事，鼓励其他合作的领导者思考自己的“鲍勃时刻”——当你意识到不告诉别人他们犯了错误是不友善的，从长远来看这没有任何好处。所以对我来说，至少这很有帮助。另一个有用的方法是，让别人专注于为他人做正确的事，而不是取悦他们。要比当下自己的不适更关心他人。与直接挑战相比，这对人们来说更容易做到。这关乎如何克服阻碍。这就是我为什么称之为“毁灭主义”。同理心是件好事，但有时同理心会让人陷入瘫痪——至少对我来说是这样，因为我太清楚自己的话可能会伤害别人，以至于我选择沉默。（01:09:00）所以当我强迫自己去做时——如果你愿意，可以称之为富有同情心的坦率，但当我不那么敏感于对方的感受时，顺便说一句，我可能常常误解对方的意图，他们会说，“没关系。”但当我放下这些顾虑，真正为对方着想，为他们的未来着想时，回到你的观点——如果你知道某人晋升至关重要，而他们若继续以某种方式与人交谈就无法晋升，那么你就专注于他们想要的东西。这真的很有助于克服这些障碍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just a few more questions before we wrap up. Your book sold something like half a million copies.
turns.zh: 在结束之前，再问几个问题。你的书销量约50万册。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: A million now.
turns.zh: 现在是100万册了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A million copies.

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Million copies. Million in 23 languages. Yes.
turns.zh: 100万册。23种语言的版本。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 23 languages. I had a stat of 20 languages. Jesus Christ. So a lot of people have read it, a lot of people have been using it. What's something that people often just get wrong that super frustrates you about the system, the recommendations that you just wish people come on, here's what I really wanted to say, or here's what you should change.
turns.zh: 23种语言。我之前统计的是20种语言。天哪。所以有很多人读过它，很多人一直在使用它。关于这个系统，关于那些推荐，有什么是人们经常误解的，让你特别抓狂的？你真希望人们能听听你真正想说的，或者你希望他们能做出哪些改变。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: There's two things. I mean, as I mentioned earlier, when you write about a book about feedback, you're going to get a lot of it. One is this, in the spirit of Radical Candor and then the person acts like a jerk. That is not the spirit of Radical Candor. That is the spirit of obnoxious aggression. But shortly after the book came out, I was giving a talk at a tech company in San Francisco and I got some feedback from the CEO of that company that was so impactful that it caused me to write my next book, which is called Radical Respect. And in many ways, Radical Respect is kind of the prequel to Radical Candor because if you don't respect the other person, it's impossible to care about them and you're not going to bother challenging them directly. So what happened in this meeting? I walked in, I was really excited to give this talk. (01:12:04): The CEO had been a colleague of mine for the better part of a decade. She's a person I like and respect enormously, and she's one of too few black women CEOs in tech or in any other sector. And when I finished giving the talk, she pulled me aside and she said, "Kim, I'm excited to roll out Radical Candor. I think it's really going to help me build the kind of career I want." But she said, "I got to tell you, it's much harder for me to roll it out than it is for you." And she went on to explain to me that as soon as she would offer folks even the most gentle, compassionate criticism, they would call her an angry black woman. And I knew this was true as soon as she said it, and I knew how unfair it was because she's like one of the most even keeled, cheerful people I've ever worked with. (01:12:49): And I realized a bunch of things at the same time when she told me that, the first was that I had not been the kind of colleague that I aspire to be, that I imagined myself to be. I had failed even to notice the extent to which she had to show up unfailingly, cheerful and pleasant in every meeting we had ever been in together even though she had what to be ticked off about as we all do at work. So I had failed to be an upstander, a good colleague. The second thing I realized was that I had also failed to acknowledge when I was experiencing different versions of bias, prejudice and bullying. And I think part of the reason it's kind of hard for the author of a book called Radical Candor to admit she was in denial. But I had been in denial about a bunch of experiences I had had in the workplace. (01:13:41): I had pretended that a whole host of things were not happening, that were in fact happening. And I think part of the reason why I did that was that I never wanted to think of myself as a victim, but even less than wanting to think of myself as a victim did I want to think of myself as the culprit. So I'd been even more deeply in denial about the times that I had said or done things that hurt other people who I worked with, said or done things that were biased or worse. I had bullied people before. And by the way, when you become a leader, you're much more prone to bullying even if you don't think of yourself as a bully, which I certainly don't think of myself as a bully, but that doesn't mean I never bullied anyone. And then the last thing I realized was that as a leader, I imagined that I was creating these BS free zones, but I had allowed all manner of BS to pass. So that was what prompted me to write the next book, Radical Respect, which you can pre-order right now and please do.
turns.zh: 主要有两点。我之前提到过，当你写一本关于反馈的书时，会收到大量反馈。其中一点是，秉承《彻底坦诚》（Radical Candor）的精神行事，却被误解为不友善的攻击。这绝非《彻底坦诚》的精神所在。但书出版后不久，我在旧金山一家科技公司做演讲时，得到的反馈让我震惊，以至于促使我写了下一本书——《彻底尊重》（Radical Respect）。从某种程度上说，《彻底尊重》是《彻底坦诚》的前传，因为若不尊重他人，就无法真正关心他们，也不会主动挑战他们。那么那次会议发生了什么？我走进会场时，满怀热情准备演讲。（01:12:04）：这位CEO曾是我近十年的同事。她是我非常敬重和欣赏的人，也是科技及其他行业中为数不多的黑人女性CEO之一。当我结束演讲后，她把我拉到一边说：“金，我很期待推广《彻底坦诚》。我觉得它真的能帮我打造理想的职业生涯。”但她说：“我得告诉你，对我来说，推广它比你难得多。”她接着解释说，只要她提出哪怕是最温和、最善意的批评，人们就会指责她是个愤怒的黑人女性。我一听就知道这是真的，也深知这有多不公平——她是我共事过最冷静、最开朗的人之一。（01:12:49）：那一刻我同时意识到几件事。首先，我没有成为自己理想中的同事。我甚至没有注意到她在我们共事的每一次会议上都要保持无比开朗和友善的面容，尽管她和我们所有人一样在工作中难免会生气。换句话说，我没有成为一个正义的旁观者，一个好同事。其次，我意识到自己也未能承认曾经历过各种形式的偏见、歧视和霸凌。我想，《彻底坦诚》的作者难以承认自己曾陷入否认状态，部分原因在于此。但我也曾否认自己在职场中经历过的种种。比如，我假装很多本该发生的事没有发生。而我这样做的原因之一，是我不想把自己视为受害者，更不想把自己视为加害者。于是，我对自己说过或做过的伤害同事、带有偏见或更糟行为的次数更是深陷否认之中。说实话，当你成为领导者后，即便你不认为自己是霸凌者（我绝对不认为自己是霸凌者），也更容易陷入霸凌行为。这让我决定写下一本书《彻底尊重》，现在就可以预购了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was my next question. Talk more about this book. What is it about? Where people find it?
turns.zh: 接下来是我的问题。多聊聊这本书吧。它讲的是什么？人们在哪里能买到它？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Radical Respect comes out in May. You can pre-order it now. Anywhere you buy books, at your local independent bookstore, I'm speaking at a conference of independent bookstore owners soon you can pre-order it on Amazon or Barnes Noble or anywhere else you buy buy books.
turns.zh: 《激进尊重》五月出版，现在可以预购了。无论你在哪里买书，无论是在当地独立书店，还是我即将参加的独立书店主会议，你都可以在亚马逊、巴诺书店或其他购书平台预购。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And who would you say it's most for?
turns.zh: 你觉得这本书最适合哪类人？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: So there are chapters in that book about things leaders can do. There are chapters in the book about things you can do if you're harmed by bias, prejudice, or bullying. There are chapters in the book about how to be a great upstander, how to be a better colleague, and there are chapters in the book about how to become part of the solution, not part of the problem when you're the culprit. And I think we all find ourselves in all four of those roles at different moments in time, and I don't think there's any one group who can solve this problem. Everyone is responsible for creating a more respectful work environment.
turns.zh: 书中有些章节讲的是领导者可以做些什么。有些章节针对因偏见、歧视或霸凌而受害的人如何自救。还有些章节教你如何成为优秀的挺身而出者、更出色的同事，以及当你是问题制造者时，如何成为解决问题的一份子。我认为我们每个人在不同时期都会扮演这四种角色中的任何一种，而且我认为没有任何一个群体能独自解决这个问题。每个人都有责任共同营造更尊重的工作环境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We'll link to that in the show notes.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们会在节目笔记中附上链接。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Amazing.
turns.zh: 太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To leave people with a very tactical next step. What's one thing they could do this week today to get better at Radical Candor, to start building that muscle?
turns.zh: 最后给大家留下一个非常实用的下一步行动建议。本周乃至今天，他们能做什么来提升“激进坦诚”能力，并开始锻炼这种能力？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: I would love it if everyone would write down their go-to question what are the words that will come out of your mouth and practice it. Practice it in front of the mirror and then practice it with a friend and refine it. Just figure out what, because it is uncomfortable to solicit feedback from others. They don't want to give it to you and you don't really want to hear it. So if everybody can write down their go-to question and then put five minutes in your calendar of someone you're going to ask that question of.
turns.zh: 我希望大家都能写下自己常用的提问方式——那些从你口中说出的关键词——并加以练习。先对着镜子练习，再找个朋友练习并完善它。关键在于，主动征求他人反馈总让人感到不适。他们不愿给出反馈，而你也不想听。所以，如果每个人都能写下自己的常用提问方式，然后在日历上为某个你要提问的人预留五分钟时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that calendar entry, I was going to come back to it actually. So you do the one-on-one agenda, adding the question, the calendar entry is for people you don't have a one-on-one with, pick someone that you're going to ask that you're not meeting with regularly.
turns.zh: 实际上我还想再提一下日历安排。你们可以把这项任务加入一对一会议的议程，同时把日历条目留给那些你没有定期会面的人。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Absolutely. Or add it to the bottom of your next one-on-one agenda. That's fair too. Either one.
turns.zh: 没错。或者把它加到下一次一对一会议的末尾。两种方式都可以。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Kim, is there anything else you want to leave folks with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 太棒了。金，在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想留给听众的吗？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: I think just remember, you do not have to choose between being successful and being a jerk. You can be a successful kind person.
turns.zh: 我觉得要记住，你不必在成功和做个混蛋之间做出选择。你可以成为成功的善良之人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, I love that. Amazing. Okay, well with that, we've reached a very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 哦，我喜欢这个观点。太棒了。好的，现在让我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节。你们准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: I'm ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books you've recommended most to other people? You've already mentioned a few but what do you want to share?
turns.zh: 你向别人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？你已经提到了一些，但还想分享些什么？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yes, I've mentioned a couple. Please do buy Radical Respect, I believe that the more novels people read, the better. People often ask me, what can I do to move up on the care personally dimension of Radical Candor and read more novels? This is the best way I know of to build compassion for other people, to understand the emotional signals that might be coming at you. I mean, some of my favorite novels are Middlemarch. I try to reread that all the time. Anything that Toni Morrison wrote, the Bluest Eye is one of my favorite, but also Song of Solomon. It just such a brilliant writer and will help you enter into the lives of people that you haven't entered into. I think that Orlando by Virginia Woolf is another one of my favorites. And Robertson Davies, the Deptford Trilogy is an incredible set of novels to read. I'm cheating now and giving you three.
turns.zh: 是的，我提过几本。请务必购买《激进的尊重》这本书，我相信人们读得小说越多越好。经常有人问我，怎样才能在《激进的坦诚》中的个人关怀维度上有所提升，同时多读些小说？这是我所知的最佳途径，能培养对他人的同理心，理解他人可能传递的情感信号。比如，我最喜欢的几部小说包括《米德尔马契》，我常反复重读。托妮·莫里森的作品，比如《最蓝的眼睛》和《所罗门之歌》，她是位才华横溢的作家，能带你深入他人的人生世界。我还很喜欢弗吉尼亚·伍尔夫的《奥兰多》，以及罗伯逊·戴维斯的《德普特福德三部曲》。这次我稍作破例，推荐三本。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The more the merrier.
turns.zh: 多多益善。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yes, Alice Walker, the Color Purple is another one of my very favorite books, so I recommend reading more novels.
turns.zh: 没错，艾丽斯·沃克的《紫色》也是我最喜欢的书之一，所以我推荐多读小说。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this leaning into fiction that doesn't come up often on this podcast, so this is great. What is a favorite recent movie or TV show that you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种深入文学创作的讨论，这在播客中不常见，真是太棒了。你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: I watched all 19 seasons of Grey's Anatomy with my daughter during and after COVID. That was really fun.
turns.zh: 新冠疫情期间和之后，我们全家一起看完了《实习医生格蕾》的前19季。这真是段美好的回忆。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Actually. I did the same thing with my wife. We didn't do all the seasons, but we watched a lot of Grey's Anatomy.
turns.zh: 实际上，我和妻子也这么做了。虽然没看完所有季，但也看了不少。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: We watched every single one. It's still coming out.
turns.zh: 我们一集不落地看完了。这部剧至今还在更新。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's funny to see which characters continue and which I die off, leave.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，看看哪些角色延续下来，哪些又离去、逝去。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 没错，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man. Okay. Funny
turns.zh: 天哪。好的。挺有意思的。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: And Shonda Rhimes, I mean, watch her TED Talk, amazing person.
turns.zh: 还有珊达·瑞姆斯，我是说，去看看她的TED演讲吧，她真是了不起的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right, we'll link to that in the show notes. Do you have a favorite interview question that you like to ask when you're interviewing people that might be helpful to folks interviewing?
turns.zh: 好的，我们会在节目笔记中附上链接。你有没有喜欢的采访问题，适合用来提问被采访者，对其他面试者也有帮助的？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: The question that I like to ask is just tell me the story of your career. And I know that's kind of, maybe it's a hard, it seems like a softball, but it's actually can be unfairly hard or not. I don't know, unfairly hard, but I always learn a lot about people from how they tell the story of their life and their career. And then what I try to do is they'll say a couple of things that really interest me and I sort of double-click down into the details of a couple of aspects. I love people's life stories, so that makes it a more fun conversation for me. Often people like talking about themselves so it's not too painful for them, but you also learn all kinds of unexpected things.
turns.zh: 我最喜欢问的问题就是：请给我讲讲你的职业生涯故事。我知道这听起来可能有点简单，是个软问题，但其实可能出乎意料地难回答。我不知道，是不是出乎意料地难，但我总能从人们讲述自己人生和职业生涯的故事中收获很多。然后我会挑出几个让我感兴趣的点，深入探讨几个方面。我喜欢人们的人生故事，所以这对我来说是更有趣的对话。通常人们喜欢谈论自己，所以对他们来说不算太难，但你也能收获各种意想不到的信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is there anything you're looking for in an answer that's like, this is a good person to hire or is it mostly information? I'm just gathering a lot of background.
turns.zh: 那你对回答有什么期待吗？比如，这是个值得雇佣的人，还是主要收集信息？我只是在收集背景资料。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: I find that I learn how the person approaches setbacks from a story, from the way they tell a story. I learn whether a person is able to identify mistakes they made. I mean, if you say, "Tell me the story of your career," if there's not a couple of mistakes in there, I also find that when they talk about accomplishments and then I double click on it, I learn a lot about what a person really did. Sometimes a person will claim credit for something that just happened that they had very little to actually to do with, and I learn about very often. I find that a good way to learn about people's skills and depth of knowledge.
turns.zh: 我发现，通过一个故事，通过讲述故事的方式，我能了解一个人如何面对挫折。我能判断一个人是否能意识到自己所犯的错误。比如，如果你问“讲讲你的职业生涯吧”，如果故事里没有几处失误，我也会发现，当他们谈及成就时，我再仔细追问，会了解到更多真实情况。有时有人会把与自己几乎无关的功劳归于自己，而我经常能识破这种虚假。我发现这是了解他人技能和知识深度的绝佳方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 你最近有没有发现什么特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yes. I love my new it's called Attitude, and they're shampoo bars and conditioner bars, so it comes in cardboard, wrapped in paper. There's no plastic. It's much more environmentally friendly, and I have long hair. It gets very tingly and the conditioner works, so I recommend.
turns.zh: 有。我超爱新买的Attitude系列洗护产品，都是洗发皂和护发皂，纸质包装，不含塑料。环保多了。我头发长，用了之后头皮很清爽，护发效果也很好，推荐一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very unique suggestion. Is there a favorite motto that you often repeat to yourself, share with people, find useful to come back to in work or in life?
turns.zh: 真是个独特的建议。有什么你常挂在嘴边、分享给他人、工作或生活中反复回味的座右铭吗？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: "It's not mean. It's clear." This is something someone told me on the streets of Manhattan. It's actually the origin story of Radical Candor. I was walking my dog, almost got hit by a cab, and this man, a perfect stranger, looked at me and he said, "I can tell you love that dog." That was all he had to do to move up on the care personally dimension, but he says, "You're going to kill that dog if you don't teach her to sit." And he pointed at the ground this kind of harsh gesture. He said, "Sit." The dog sat, had no idea she even knew what that meant. And I kind of looked up at him in amazement and he said, "It's not mean. It's clear." And then the light changed and he walked off leaving me with words to live by. So I think about that stranger all the time.
turns.zh: “这不是刻薄，这是清晰。”这是我在曼哈顿街头听到的一句话。它其实是《激进坦诚》的起源故事。我当时在遛狗，差点被出租车撞到，一个完全陌生的人看着我说：“看得出来你很爱这只狗。”这句话就足以让他在“个人关怀”维度得分飙升，但他接着说：“如果你不教它坐下，它会把你累坏的。”他用那种严厉的手势指着地面：“坐下。”狗狗乖乖坐下，压根不知道这意味着什么。我惊讶地抬头看他，他说：“这不是刻薄，这是清晰。”绿灯亮了，他走开了，却留给我一生的启示。所以我时常想起那个陌生人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a good story. Final question. I read online that you started a diamond cutting factory in Moscow at some point in your life. Can you please explain this part of your life?
turns.zh: 真是个精彩的故事。最后一个问题。我在网上看到你曾在莫斯科开过一家切割钻石的工厂，能讲讲这段经历吗？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yes. So I studied Russian literature in college, very practical major. And then I moved to what was then the Soviet Union in 1990 when I graduated from college, and I wound up taking a job with, first of all, I was with an investment company and then they pulled out of Russia and put the money in China. And so I wanted to stay in Russia and through a friend of a friend, I got a job working for this diamond company called Lazare Kaplan, new York-based diamond company, and they were trying to figure out what they should do in Russia. And I found out there was an opportunity to start this diamond cutting factory. And it was actually my first management job because I had to hire these diamond cutters and I had to hire them away from these Russian diamond cutting factories and I knew nothing about management or business or anything. (01:23:44): I'd studied Russian literature. I knew a lot about Dostoyevsky, so I thought it was going to be easy though. I was like, well, the ruble is collapsing. I'm going to pay them in dollars. Of course they'll come work for me. But they didn't take the job right away. To my surprise, they wanted to have a picnic. And at the picnic we brought a bottle of vodka, and there's a rule in Russia, if you open a bottle, you got to finish the bottle. (01:24:07): So by the end of the bottle of vodka, I realized that what I could offer that the state could not offer them was to give a damn about them. They wanted to know that I would be a manager who would get them out of Russia if things went sideways there. And as you can imagine, I've been thinking a lot about, they were all men, about these men because I haven't been able to get them out. And I'm devastated by what Russia has done to Ukraine, but that was the moment when I realized that management really matters, and that to be good at it, you have to care about other people. And that was what made it interesting to me.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我在大学学的是俄罗斯文学，专业很实用。1990年大学毕业后，我搬到了当时的苏联，最终在一家投资公司工作，但他们后来撤出了俄罗斯，把资金投到了中国。于是我想留在俄罗斯，通过朋友的朋友，我在纽约的钻石公司Lazare Kaplan找到了工作，负责俄罗斯的钻石切割业务。当时他们正试图在俄罗斯开展业务，而我发现有机会开办一家钻石切割工厂。这实际上是我的第一份管理工作，因为我需要从俄罗斯的钻石切割厂招募员工，而我对管理、商业一窍不通。（01:23:44）：我学过俄罗斯文学，对陀思妥耶夫斯基很了解，本以为会很轻松。但当时卢布正在贬值，我想用美元支付工资，结果他们不愿接受。令我惊讶的是，他们想先开个野餐会。野餐会上我们带了一瓶伏特加，而俄罗斯有个规矩，打开瓶子就必须喝完。（01:24:07）：喝完那瓶伏特加后，我意识到相比国家，我能为他们提供的，是真心关心他们的处境。他们希望我能在俄罗斯局势恶化时带他们离开。可以想象，当时全是男性员工，我至今仍为未能成功撤离他们而感到痛心。乌克兰被俄罗斯侵略，这让我深刻认识到管理的核心在于关爱他人。也正因如此，这次对话对我来说意义非凡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Man, that is a heavy first job as a manager.
turns.zh: 天哪，管理层的首份工作可真是艰难啊。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Yeah. Yes, it was.
turns.zh: 是的，确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, Kim, this was awesome. I think we're going to help a lot of people become better leaders. I think we're going to help a lot of companies change their culture. I'm so honored that you agreed to do this. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to follow up and learn more about your stuff? And then two, how can listeners be helpful to you?
turns.zh: 哇，金，这次对话太棒了。我相信我们能帮助很多领导者提升管理能力，也能助力许多公司改变文化。很荣幸你能接受这次采访。最后两个问题：如果听众想了解更多内容，可以在哪里找到你？还有，听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Radicalcandor.com is our website, and I'm not much on Twitter slash X anymore, but you can find us. We do a lot of posting on LinkedIn. I think that the thing that people can help me do is to send us a note. You can also email us radicalcandor@radicalcandor.com and let us know what could we do in podcasts like this or in our materials? What could we do that would make it easier for you to put these ideas into practice? Because Radical Candor is, it's about behavior change, and it sounds easy, but it's really hard, and we're always trying to figure out how to help people walk the talk here.
turns.zh: 我们的网站是radicalcandor.com。我现在不怎么玩推特或X了，但可以在领英上找到我们。读者可以给我们发邮件至radicalcandor@radicalcandor.com，告诉我们在播客或资料中可以如何改进，让实践更容易。比如，Radical Candor关注的是行为改变，听起来简单，但实际很难。我们一直在探索如何帮助人们将理念付诸实践。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think doing this podcast is going to make a dent in that goal.
turns.zh: 我觉得做这个播客会对实现这个目标有所助益。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Oh, good.
turns.zh: 太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kim, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 金，非常感谢你今天的参与。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Thank you. I really enjoyed it.
turns.zh: 谢谢。我真的很享受这次对话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Same. Bye everyone.
turns.zh: 我也是。再见大家。

turns.speaker: Kim Scott
turns.en: Take care everyone.
turns.zh: 大家保重。
